purpose: The Resource Use Explorer model: every number the page uses, with its low, high, kind, and evidence ids, and every row at the default settings. Modeled estimates, not measurements.
said_aloud: Every unit of work pays its own energy plus its share of the hardware that sits idle waiting for it; where it runs sets the carbon and the water, judged on one grid for both sides of any comparison; and who bills it sets the price, named by its basis and never ranked across bases.
baseline: One person-hour of use on the whole chain (data center or node, network, home router, device), in watt-hours, with price, CO2e, and water printed for the same hour. Each row keeps its natural unit and reaches the hour through a stated rate the reader can change. Stored data has no hour: it is reported in terabyte-years with the copies stated. Architecture comparisons use one organization-year. A million tokens stays beneath the hour as the AI-only cross-vendor unit, with the warning that per-token coefficients are one vendor framework's defaults and that a Tribal-language prompt can cost up to 179 times English (au-026).
range_label: Ranges are every input's low and high run through the same equations with the settings fixed: a spread, not a confidence interval.

Jegham is a preprint that Joule says overstates production figures by 4 to 20 times (fp-020). A multi-turn chat carries growing context and agents make about 12 model calls per typed prompt (fp-031); no source counts model calls per chat prompt.

grid_dc.label: Grid for the data center and network (the same feeds as the node, so neither side gets a feed the other cannot)
grid_dc.why: Carbon is location-based only. Average, short-run margin, and long-run margin differ nine times for the same kilowatt-hour in the Northwest, so the choice is printed on the figure. Hydro, wind, and solar are life-cycle factors (gf-035, gf-034, gf-033) while eGRID rates count combustion only, and a feed is a declared supply arrangement, not a location factor, unless the machine is physically behind that meter; hydro already committed elsewhere is not clean new supply. Wind, solar, and diesel print no generation water until a claim for them is added. Washington's in-state rate is CO2, not CO2e, and includes exports. The BPA factor is regulator-assigned for power bought from BPA, on a different accounting method from eGRID, so the gap between the two is not a grid effect.

Availability and redundancy: one box, one link, ten operators.

Maturity and support of the named open-source apps (sf-057, lf-055, sf-055).
ai_is_not_data_centers: In the same hour the screen and router are about 12 Wh on every phone row with the router charged by time (a television alone is 100 Wh or more), and the activity adds 0.8 to 3 Wh, chat or video.

Most data center electricity is not AI today, on two definitions that must not be mixed: AI-focused facilities were 155 of 485 TWh worldwide in 2025 (32 percent, lf-001, IEA) and AI workloads 15 to 25 percent (lf-002, second-hand). The growth is AI: AI-focused facilities are 310 of the 460 TWh the IEA adds by 2030 (67 percent, lf-001), and in LBNL's US reference case AI servers reach 55 percent of data center energy in 2030 (lf-003); training is 20 to 35 percent of AI server draw (lf-004).

AI can run outside a data center: the place profile moves 1,000 prompts from 300 Wh in a hyperscaler to 24 Wh on laptops that are on anyway, at a cost in quality, and 11 to 29 percent of queries go to the cloud regardless (sf-035). A busy data center has the lowest energy per answer at equal model size because its hardware sits idle least; that is arithmetic about utilization, not a reason to site one, and a dedicated local node catches up only above about 2.8 million prompts a year on one grid.
Data centers run things that are not AI: the video, storage, office, and search rows.

One person's chat is not the buildout: all of ChatGPT's text chat is about 0.27 TWh a year on Google's median prompt (0.22 to 0.55 across the median figures), text only, a floor for one product against the IEA's 485 TWh global total. A proposed building is a question for the project scale panel and the Questions for Tribal Leaders, and hosting a building does not supply a Nation's own computing: those are separate decisions.
qualitative.rebound: Rebound is outside the unit: per-task energy falls 10 times a year (ec-057; Google 33 times, fp-009) while totals rise (Google plus 37 percent, rs-003), price elasticity sits near one at the provider level (ec-044), and the IEA says so (ec-058). The page prints the per-unit number and the count beside it, and this pair as the reason a per-unit saving is not a total one.

disclaimer: These are modeled estimates, not measurements, from an open-book model checked against published figures: every input is a published figure or a labeled assumption, shown with its receipt, every other number is arithmetic on those inputs, and nothing is fitted. In technical terms it is a bottom-up engineering model; it estimates no coefficient from data, so it is not econometric. Its ranges are spreads, not distributions. Each row is units of work times published coefficients, plus the share of hardware that sits idle to serve it, scaled by the building and the grid where it runs. No vendor has published a measured production figure for most rows, no Tribally owned facility in the record has published its electricity use or total water, and the back-test printed here shows where the model lands within a factor of two and where it misses by five to eight. Change a setting and the answer changes; that is the point of the tool. It says nothing about any site, stream, rate class, or Treaty-reserved right, and it never turns sovereignty, consent, or resilience into a number.
